page: Amazon Web Services x1e.xlarge is a memory-optimized instance built on the x86_64 architecture. It features an Intel Xeon E7-8880 v3 processor running at 2.3 GHz, delivering 4 dedicated vCPUs across 2 physical cores with hyper-threading enabled. The instance is equipped with 122.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-core ratio of 30.5 GB per core. Local storage is provided via a 120 GB NVMe SSD, and network connectivity is configured with a baseline bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Benchmark data indicates that the instance prioritizes memory capacity over raw processing speed. CPU-bound performance is limited, with stress-ng single-core and multi-core metrics falling into the bottom 10% of tested hardware. Similarly, Geekbench single-core and multi-core scores are positioned in the bottom 10%. Memory bandwidth tests show a read-only small block cached speed of 156.24 GB/sec (bottom 25%), while large-block uncached read and write speeds drop to 19.06 GB/sec and 13.67 GB/sec respectively (bottom 10%).

The primary tradeoff of the x1e.xlarge is its low compute-to-memory ratio, making it less suitable for CPU-intensive tasks like software compilation or heavy cryptography, which scored in the bottom 10% to 25% in Passmark testing. However, the 122.0 GB RAM capacity and local NVMe SSD storage make it a viable option for memory-intensive workloads that do not require high CPU throughput. Appropriate workloads include in-memory databases, caching layers, and enterprise applications requiring large memory footprints with modest processing demands.
description: Amazon Web Services x1e.xlarge is a memory-optimized instance designed for workloads requiring a high memory-to-vCPU ratio. Powered by an Intel Xeon E7-8880 v3 processor running at 2.3 GHz, it provides 4 dedicated vCPUs and 122.0 GB of RAM, resulting in 30.5 GB of memory per core. The instance includes a 120 GB NVMe SSD for local storage and a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps. Benchmark results show limited CPU and memory bandwidth performance, with stress-ng and Geekbench scores placing in the bottom 10% to 25% of tested servers. Consequently, this instance is best suited for memory-intensive applications with low compute requirements, such as small in-memory databases, caching layers, and legacy enterprise applications that demand substantial memory capacity without intensive processing needs.
